claims.text: A machine-learning model integrating temperature-dependent electron–phonon and defect scattering parameters will improve conductivity-prediction accuracy for bulk HfNbTaTiZr over conventional analytical models.
Explicit correction factors can represent scattering caused by 1 wt.% oxygen in HfNbTaTiZr.
The material states considered are nominally pristine HfNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
The pristine HfNbTaTiZr state is an ideal defect-free material.
The proposed model will use ab initio correction factors for defect and impurity scattering together with temperature-dependent scattering rates.
The model is intended to cover 0–200 K and 300–1200 K for both pristine and 1 wt.% oxygen-containing samples.
Electron–phonon interactions and defects, including oxygen impurities, produce temperature-dependent scattering rates relevant to electrical conduction.
Directly representing lattice-vibration and defect or impurity scattering will more accurately reproduce measured temperature-dependent electron conduction.
The model will predict electrical conductivity within approximately 20% of experiment in both specified temperature regimes.
The proposed model will outperform conventional analytical conductivity predictions based on a perfect crystal lattice.
Existing analytical predictions for this problem assume defect-free crystals.
Existing analytical predictions fail to capture additional scattering from 1 wt.% oxygen and other defects.
Existing analytical models typically deviate from measured HfNbTaTiZr conductivity more than the proposed model will.
The claimed applicability is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing up to 1 wt.% oxygen and temperatures of 0–200 K or 300–1200 K.
Performance outside the specified temperature intervals or at substantially different impurity concentrations is untested.
Prior work has applied machine learning to related high-entropy or refractory concentrated alloy datasets.
The cited prior machine-learning applications support an approximately 20% conductivity-accuracy target for HfNbTaTiZr.
The exact improvement depends on calibration quality and accurate determination of defect-scattering parameters.
Conductivity measurements at 150 K and 900 K for pristine and oxygen-containing specimens will be held out from model calibration.
A prediction error greater than 20% at either held-out temperature will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome defines approximately 20% as an absolute error relative to experiment, whereas the uncertainty field describes approximately 20% as an accuracy improvement over a baseline. These are different performance metrics.
